utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Registrar -- just a moment, could you please state which case number this is and ask the accused to enter?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-9-PT, the Prosecutor against Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Now, you can ask Mr Simic to be brought in. We will wait for him to take the seat. In the meantime, who appears on behalf of the Prosecution in this matter, please? This is Ms Paterson, but she will tell us for herself and she will tell us who assists her.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It is Nancy Paterson representing the Prosecution. I am the only attorney here today for the Prosecution. My assistant is the case manager, Ms Verhaag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we turn to the Defence, Mr Simic, would you please take your earphones now? Could the security officer help Mr Simic to take the earphones? Can you hear me, Mr Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Who appears for the Defence, please, because I would like some details here? Normally, it should be Mr Drago Vukovic who represents the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am Drago Vukovic, attorney from Belgrade, along with my colleague, Mr Pisarevic and Mr Pantelic, who agreed on a pro bono basis to help me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you please remind me the names of your colleagues? I know Mr Pantelic well, but on your left-hand side, could you tell me who is your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is Mr Pisarevic and Mr Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There are three of you. Could you please give the Trial Chamber some explanations, because I think that you were the only counsel that was appointed. Could you give us some additional explanations about this fact, that you are three?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Pisarevic and Mr Pantelic are here present as initial attorneys for Mr Simic -- in fact, Mr Pisarevic took part in the surrender and the transfer of Mr Simic to The Hague and to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, and Mr Pantelic also took part in this process. So, on this basis, they are together present, and are assisting me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr Simic, is it your desire just for today -- could you please explain what is your position? Please be seated, Mr Vukovic. Mr Vukovic, you can be seated. Mr Simic, can you tell us what is your attitude? You have three counsel today. You were appointed one counsel by the Tribunal. Please explain? Could you put the microphone on? Could you please explain the situation about your counsel. There are three counsel for you -- you had only one, and now you have three people representing you. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Vukovic is my Defence attorney. He was assigned to me by the Tribunal, and Mr Pisarevic comes from the same town that I come from, and is completely abreast of all developments in this case, and has been coming to The Hague to prepare in the conditions. As far as the Rules of the Tribunal that only one attorney may represent one accused, Mr Pisarevic is involved in another case and Mr Pantelic is also involved in a case of Mr Jelisic. However, they are completely familiar with all the developments so far in this case and Mr Vukovic is a new attorney who has been assigned to me, whereas Mr Pantelic and Mr Pisarevic have been familiar with all the proceedings so far, and this is why I have asked them to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the Registrar tell us whether you have any particular remarks you would like to make, because this concerns particularly your Office?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the particular remark would be that a Registrar cannot assign more than one counsel -- in this case it is Mr Vukovic, so the Registry can only take note that there are two other counsel here on a pro bono basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, I will consult my colleagues now. (Pause). The judges of this Trial Chamber have found out that it is a choice of the accused -- the choice of Mr Simic concern only this motion hearing for provisional release, and that is why the judges will accept this situation. The judges take note that there are no additional fees or no additional costs for the Registry, and that the accused cannot repeat this situation on another occasion, so this is a unique situation that will apply only for today. So, the judges would like that Mr Vukovic from now on takes the Defence and pleads, so in case this time round, Mr Vukovic, you need to consult your colleagues, please feel free to do so. Can we now take up the motion hearing on provisional release and I will give the floor, first, to Mr Vukovic and, after that, we will ask the Prosecution bench to explain their observations. Mr Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My colleague tells me that in case you would like to feel more comfortable, you may use the microphone that is in front of Mr Pantelic and he will certainly lend it to you. It will be much easier and you will not have to bend so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, on 17 March of this year, the Defence submitted a motion for provisional release of the accused, Milan Simic, and, with your Honours' permission, I would just like to state for the public record the basic submissions contained in this motion. First of all, I would like to point out that Milan Simic voluntarily and unconditionally surrendered to this Tribunal on 14 February 1998. During the initial appearance before the Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor, through its representative, pressed its positive position in regard to provisional release and then, pursuant to Rule 65, four conditions need to be met for the provisional release and those are exceptional circumstances, guarantee that the accused will appear for trial and that, if released, he will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person, as well as the approval of the host country. I will now try to set out that all these four conditions have been met. As far as the exceptional circumstances are concerned, Mr Simic is a seriously disabled person, he is hemiplegic, he is bound to a wheelchair, he has no use of his legs and he has still got a bullet lodged in his spine, he has the use of only one kidney and one arm and, therefore, he requires special conditions for his normal life. He also requires assistance of highly specialised medical personnel in order to conduct his daily life, and he has been in this condition since the day he was wounded. I am only going to point out some problems that he meets daily in the detention unit and I would like to give Mr Simic an opportunity to personally tell you what sort of problems he encounters on a daily basis in the detention unit. First of all, he needs to go to the hospital every day at 5 o'clock in the afternoon. He goes there and, until this time, he is isolated from the rest of the detainees in the detention unit, so that, during the period of time which is their free time for them, which is 5.30 until 8.30 in the evening, he cannot socialise with them. Every morning he arrives in the detention unit around 8.30, and he spends additional two hours alone by himself, because he is unable to take daily walks and, also, he, during the lunch period, also remains detained. While in the detention unit, he is unable to take regular rests, because there are no -- he has no conditions to lie down, so that, throughout the day, he is bound to his wheelchair, which causes him unnecessary pain. Also, the layout of the detention unit is such that he cannot approach the toilet facilities or the wash basin in his wheelchair, so that he can only get some assistance from Mr Saric and Mr Tadic who are from his home town and who have made efforts to assist him, and I will leave Mr Simic to elucidate further issues in this matter. The next condition is the danger that he will not appear for trial, that is, that he will escape. The Defence points out that the accused surrendered voluntarily, that he chose to place himself under the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, and this proves that he is willing to appear at trial as well as all additional hearings, and he will answer any summons of the Tribunal to appear for any portion of the proceedings. Also, as a disabled person bound to a wheelchair, that implies that he would need much greater effort and that it would be much more difficult for him to try to escape and fail to appear before the Trial Chamber. As far as the third condition is concerned, that is, that he may pose a threat to the victims or witnesses, the Defence would like to point out that Mr Simic is a family man, he lives with his wife. His wife is a pillar in his life and she helps him daily to get through the difficulties. She is a very popular person among the citizens of her home town and, also, in his family. Mr Simic, furthermore, has never been criminally prosecuted before, and, as a disabled person, and given his character, he would not present a threat or danger to any person with whom he may come into contact. I would also like to point out that the accused has also given a written statement, which he is prepared to repeat orally, that he commits to not coming into contact with any potential witness or other co-accused, so we believe that this condition of Rule 65(B) has also been met. As far as the acceptance of the host country is concerned, we believe that, based on the past practice of the Tribunal, should the Trial Chamber come to the position that all other conditions for provisional release of Mr Simic have been met, that the host country will also go along with this decision. Finally, we submit that all conditions provided by Rule 65(B) have been met and, as the Office of the Prosecutor also supported our motion for provisional release, and in the letter of 12 March 1998 in which the Defence asked for the provisional release and the OTP has responded favourably to that. Furthermore, the Prime Minister of the Republika Srbska, Mr Dodik, and Minister Stankovic have also provided assurance to the Tribunal regarding the provisional release of Mr Simic, and have assured the Tribunal that they will take all necessary measures to assure the provisional release of Mr Simic and will post a bond of $US25,000 should Mr Simic fail to appear at trial, as well as on the basis that Mr Simic himself gave a written statement, which he will confirm here orally, that he understands all the conditions set out in the letter from 12 March 1998. The Defence respectfully requests that the motion for provisional release of Mr Simic be granted for humanitarian reasons because the health conditions of Mr Simic are too difficult for Mr Simic to bear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Vukovic. I am turning now to Ms Paterson and I would like to see what the Office of the Prosecutor thinks of this matter. Maybe you can complete -- we know the basis of your position, but maybe you can complete it now. You have, during the initial appearance, already indicated what your position would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. As has been stated, the Prosecution mentioned at the initial appearance that, if we could receive sufficient assurances that Mr Simic would return for trial, we would look favourably on this motion. We have worked for the last several weeks quite amicably with the Defence towards this end and we think that we have reached a point where we have now received the assurances and guarantees that we find acceptable. As Mr Vukovic said, pursuant to Rule 65(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, if an accused can establish that exceptional circumstances attach to the case, the Trial Chamber may order the provisional release of the accused prior to trial, if the Chamber is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person. The Prosecutor is satisfied that, having regard to the accused's serious physical handicaps caused as a result of a shooting incident in February 1993, Milan Simic does meet the exceptional circumstances test for provisional release. This opinion has been formed after conferring with the accused's Defence counsel and representatives of the ICTY detention unit and after reviewing the accused's medical records. While the accused himself, we believe, will acknowledge that he has received the best care available by the staff of the detention unit, it is clear that the medical and physical facilities of the detention unit cannot adequately meet the demands of the accused's physical condition. Due to the limited resources of the detention unit, which are already stretched to the maximum, the Prosecutor believes that it will be in the best interests of the defendant to return to Bosanski Samac where special physical provisions have been made for his care. In order to satisfy the Prosecutor that sufficient guarantees were in place to assure the return of the accused, and to monitor his presence at his home at Bosanski Samac on a daily basis, as Mr Vukovic has said, a letter of assurance was signed by Prime Minister Dodik and the Minister of Interior, Stankovic, of the Republika Srbska, in which they both agreed to guarantee the accused's return to the Tribunal for his trial and for any other pre-trial hearings that the Trial Chamber may order. Furthermore, a set of detailed conditions has been granted which, among other things, sets out some procedure by which the local police and the IPTF will monitor Mr Simic's physical presence at his home in Bosanski Samac on a daily basis. The Prosecutor would like to note that she feels that the agreements reached in regard to these assurances and conditions, secured from the authorities of Republika Srbska, represent a significant advance in the relationship and cooperation between the Tribunal and Republika Srbska. By signing the letter of assurance Prime Minister Dodik and Minister of Interior Stankovic have acknowledged the jurisdiction of the Tribunal to prosecute the accused and they have stated their commitment to respect and abide by any orders issued by the Tribunal in regard to this case. It must be stressed, however, that the fact that the accused is being provisionally released should not be interpreted to mean that the Prosecution does not intend to proceed to trial and to vigorously prosecute this case. Prior to rejecting a plea offer made by the Prosecution, Milan Simic was informed that the Prosecution has significant evidence against him, and that, should he reject the plea offer, the Prosecution intended to amend the indictment and add additional charges against him for other beatings inflicted on additional victims. This course of action will be followed as stated. Despite the strong case against Mr Simic the Prosecutor is satisfied that due to his physical disabilities, the accused does not pose a threat to any of the Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecution is also satisfied that Mr Simic does intend to return to the court to defend the charges against him, and he is aware of the fact that when he returns, he will have to surrender himself to the ICTY detention unit where he will remain for the duration of the trial. As Mr Vukovic has stated, Prime Minister Dodik and Minister of Interior Stankovic have signed a letter of assurance which was drafted by the Office of the Prosecutor. That document has been signed. I believe Mr Vukovic has the original and copies have been provided to the court. In addition, the Prosecution has drafted a number of conditions, the majority of which were discussed with the Defence counsel and with Mr Simic prior to court with only a few very minor changes. I have that document with me today and we would like to have Mr Simic and Mr Vukovic sign that today here in the court. In addition, I am informed by the Registrar that the Defence has secured a bail bond or a bank letter of guarantee for the amount of $US25,000 which they are prepared to post with the Registrar, which will be payable to the Registrar of the Tribunal, should Mr Simic fail to return for trial. Finally, I am also informed by the Registrar that they have received I believe documentation from the host country that, if these proceedings are approved by the Trial Chamber, that they have no objection to the provisional release of this defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms Paterson. Before asking for additional explanations, I will turn to Mr Simic. Mr Simic, you have heard what your counsel has stated and I think that he said that you also wanted to add something. You have heard the Prosecution. So could you tell us what is your point of view, first of all, of your physical state, which is the basis of this request, and also something about a commitment you have made? Can you solemnly commit yourself to the requests of this Trial Chamber? Mr Simic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me an opportunity to say a few words. I would first like to state that I am very happy that, with respect to the OTP and the Defence, that everybody is aware of the fact that the conditions for my staying in the detention unit are not adequate. I would not like to burden you with additional details about the conditions that I daily have to fight against and I am just going to point out that I only fear that I may suffer decubitus, which is open wounds on my legs, which are immovable. This is the worst thing that can affect a paraplegic person. I have had no such problems before I arrived in The Hague, and, unfortunately, a few days ago, I did get an open wound a few days ago, which is why I had to appear here in slippers today. This just illustrates the inadequate conditions that I am faced with in the detention unit. If needed, I can provide many additional details about my health condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, Mr Simic, we do not need to have any details. This is a public hearing, so there is no need to go into any details. Your counsel gave us enough information and so we are fully aware of the physical condition you are in, and your situation in the detention unit. We are aware of your difficulties. I would like to insist on the guarantees that you gave. The Prosecutor mentioned the possibility of pressing additional charges against you and amending the indictment. I would like to know how are you going to be represented once the trial starts, because this trial is going to take place. Could you tell us something about your solemn commitment that you will be represented and how do you see this solemn commitment before the trial and your being represented there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: I have been prepared for this from the beginning. I am prepared to proceed to trial and this is why I voluntarily surrendered here -- I want to be tried here as soon as possible. There is absolutely no problem for me to appear before this Trial Chamber whenever necessary. I am hopeful that at least some basic things may be resolved in the detention unit prior to my next appearance there. I realise that these conditions cannot be made perfect, but I would hope that certain conditions may be improved so that my stay there may be made easier. As far as my appearance here is concerned, I 100 per cent assure the Tribunal that I will reappear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like to turn to the Registry and we know that, by experience, the trials here can take some time. Mr Registrar, today, when the trial date will be set, do you think that conditions in the detention unit can be changed so that the accused does not find himself in exactly the same situation -- if this Trial Chamber grants the provisional release for Mr Simic can you tell us how the situation will look like when he comes back for trial?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Registry has enough time to modify the detention cell and adapt it to the needs of Mr Simic, but, nevertheless, we do need some time that will allow us to appropriately adapt the detention cell. We have to say that the conditions of Mr Simic were unknown to us prior to his arrival at The Hague. We have already made some dispositions to adapt cells for his particular situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As you already have the floor, Mr Registrar, can you tell us about the bail bond of $25,000; what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is a letter of assurance, which is a formal commitment made by the representatives of the Republika Srbska -- this is not a guarantee deposit in cash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Registrar. This is not a proper bail and it is not actually given by the accused. In a traditional system where I come from, once somebody is granted bail, this sum is an important sum of money, which is provided by the accused and, first of all, it is the accused who gave away this sum of money and so he commits himself not to lose this considerable sum of money. Could you tell us, you were the one who negotiated this with the authorities of Republika Srbska and I have here the letter of the correspondence where we have the signatures of the Prime Minister Mr Dodik and the Minister of the Interior, Mr Stankovic. We have some problems here with the technology. We have something called bail -- what we call "bail" in my country, the sum of money is very important and is always given by the accused, as far as I know. The accused has not disposed of $25,000. Ms Paterson, could you tell us more about it. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: It has been explained to me that the different judicial systems do have different approaches to this issue. I approached the Registrar prior to finalising these agreements and asked them to look into the matter of what was appropriate, and what was going to be satisfactory to the Registrar -- whether it should be a bank letter of credit, a bail bond as we know it in the system that I am familiar with, or whether in fact it should be a cash deposit. As the court knows, Mr Simic has filed notice with the court that he has declared himself indigent and does not have enough money to pay for his attorneys, so clearly he cannot personally pose $US25,000 as bail. When this issue was discussed with the Prosecutor, she felt that it was an additional necessity for her to be satisfied that Mr Simic would return and that we had sufficient assurances of a return, that this bail bond be posted. The reason we are using the terminology "bail bond", is because that is the terminology that is used in the Statute. In Rule 65(C) it states that the Trial Chamber may impose such conditions upon the release of the accused as it may determine appropriate, including the execution of a bail bond and the observance of such conditions as are necessary to ensure his presence for trial, and the protection of others. During my discussions with Defence counsel, I informed them that the issue concerning the posting of the bail bond was entirely up to the Registrar and to the Trial Chamber, that the decision was to be made by the Trial Chamber, and that in addition to being prepared to post the bail bond, that they should also be prepared for the possibility of needing to supply a cash deposit, because, if that is what was more acceptable to the Trial Chamber, then obviously that is your decision to make. I believe that the Registrar determined that, because the Statute states "bail bond", presumably such a document should be acceptable to the court. So, this is the reason why we have pursued the procedures that we have. The reason that Mr Simic is not posting the money is that he has declared himself indigent and the Government of Republika Srbska, along with the assurance of Mr Dodik and Mr Stankovic have also agreed to post this money as a further guarantee that they will stand behind their statement that Mr Simic will return to the court. However, we leave it up to the discretion of the Trial Chamber what form of posting the Chamber finds most appropriate, be it a bail bond, a bank letter of credit, or a cash deposit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanations. I will now consult my colleagues. Would you like to ask any questions? Judge Rodrigues? Does the Registry have any remarks to make, because these are different points we address here for the first time? Yes, Mr Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is something I would like to spell out, nevertheless. According to our rules, the financial rules of the United Nations, we are not allowed to cash such a sum -- no sum at all really, not even on a temporary basis. As we have a third party who is paying and its liquidity is not in doubt, so we have come to the conclusion that the practice current in a number of States is enough, because there is personal appreciation. I think that is due to the fact that the United Nations deemed that the countries have always cooperated with the United Nations Tribunal, so that is the reason for it. Do you have anything to add before the end of our hearing, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are there any additional remarks? Ms Paterson, maybe you have a final remark to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I do not know what procedure you were planning to follow, Mr President. I would like to have just to go through the procedure of having the Defence file with the court the original of the assurance and then I would like to have the conditions that we have drafted signed here in court by Mr Simic and I would ask that the two documents either be read into the record, or that, similar to a type of a plea --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, the letter of assurance -- it is the Defence who got it or the Prosecutor -- who has this letter? Mr Vukovic, do you have the letter of assurance? I have a translation of it. I think we were given this by the translation services. It is a letter of assurance by the authorities of Republika Srbska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Defence is in the possession of the original of this letter, which it will now submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can file it with the Registrar. They will give it to the Trial Chamber. When it comes to the conditions, could you, Ms Paterson, say or remind us of the obligations that Mr Simic undertakes to abide by? Ms Paterson, could you remind us of those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: I will read the conditions to the court. This document is entitled "Conditions for the Provisional Release of Milan Simic": "Pursuant to Rule 65(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence (the Rules), Milan Simic undertakes that, if provisionally released from custody prior to trial, he will: (1) waive his right to appear at all pre-trial proceedings; (2) return to The Hague and surrender himself to the custody of the detention unit of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) to be present for any pre-trial proceeding if ordered to attend by the Trial Chamber; and (3) return to The Hague and surrender himself to the custody of the ICTY detention unit two weeks prior to the beginning of the trial. Furthermore, Milan Simic undertakes that, if provisionally released from custody prior to trial, he will observe all of the following conditions: (1) return to and remain within the confines of the municipality of Bosanski Samac; (2) upon arrival in Bosanski Samac, surrender his passport to the International Police Task Force (IPTF) office responsible for the municipality of Bosanski Samac who will then turn the passport over to the Office of the Prosecutor who will maintain control of the passport until needed; (3) meet once a day with the local Bosanski Samac police, who will maintain a log and file a daily written report confirming accused's presence at his residence every day until his return to The Hague; (4) not have contact in any manner whatsoever with any of the co-accused, specifically Slobodan Miljkovic, Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, Stevan Todorovic or Simo Zaric; (5) not have any contact whatsoever with any Prosecution witnesses for his trial (the names of whom will have been provided to his Defence counsel pursuant to the Rules); (6) will assume responsibility for all expenses regarding transportation to Bosanski Samac and back to The Hague by mode of transportation previously agreed to by the Registrar of the ICTY. Furthermore, Milan Simic undertakes that, if provisionally released from custody prior to trial, he will be obligated, in case of default on any of the above conditions, for payment to the Registrar of the ICTY of the amount of $US25,000 secured by a bail bond posted with the Registry by representatives of the entity known as Republika Srbska. Furthermore --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are speaking about guarantee, these assurances -- okay, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: "Furthermore, Milan Simic understands that: The IPTF officers responsible for the municipality of Bosanski Samac will check the log and written reports of the Bosanski Samac police on a weekly basis, may personally visit the accused once a week if they so choose, and have permission to make additional unannounced visits to the accused's residence to confirm his presence; The IPTF office responsible for the municipality of Bosanski Samac will review the records and logs kept by the local police and will provide relevant information to the OTP regarding the proper maintenance of the records and logs. Furthermore, Milan Simic understands that: (1) should he require medical treatment outside the confines of the municipality of Bosanski Samac he will file a written request for permission to leave the municipality with the Trial Chamber and said request must be approved in writing prior to his departure from the municipality; (2) should he require emergency medical treatment of such urgency that a written request for permission to leave the municipality cannot be obtained, prior to his departure from the municipality the Registrar of the ICTY and the IPTF office responsible for the municipality of Bosanski Samac must be notified by telephone of the reasons for his departure and his destination; (3) failure to comply with any of these provisions will constitute an immediate violation of this agreement and will give the OTP the right to demand the immediate return of the accused to the ICTY detention centre in The Hague; (4) failure to comply with any of these provisions will constitute an immediate violation of this agreement and will give the OTP the right to demand the immediate forfeiture of the bail bond in the amount of $US25,000 posted with the Registry by representatives of the entity known as Republika Srbska; and (5) should the accused or any of the relevant authorities of the Republika Srbska fail to abide by this agreement, such failure will be reported immediately to the office of the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Office of the High Representative then may undertake whatever actions it deems appropriate in regard to the failure of the representatives of Republika Srbska to abide by this agreement and SFOR will then have full authority to detain Milan Simic by whatever means necessary and thereafter transfer him as soon as practicable to the custody of the OTP of the ICTY for transfer back to The Hague." We ask this document be signed by both Mr Simic and Mr Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, this document will be signed. I suppose you would like it to be signed straight away. We could maybe ask the Registry to pass it on to Mr Simic and Mr Vukovic. I would nevertheless like to ask the Registry to enquire about the actual providing of this cash deposit or the bail bonds. Do you have any additional remarks to make, Mr Vukovic, which does not give us any indications of the final decision, final ruling of the judges. It is something that is only going to be taken into account when the judges are going to rule on provisional release of the accused. Ms Paterson, do you have any additional remarks to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Just, Mr President, if you would also bear with me, I would like to read into the record the exact wording of the assurance that was signed by Prime Minister Dodik and Mr Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is alright. This is a public hearing. I think it is a good thing to do, but once a document will be signed, I would like it to be filed with the Registry. Ms Paterson, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr President. This document is entitled, "Assurance of the Authorities of Republika Srbska Regarding the Provisional Release of Milan Simic": "Milan Simic, son of Vojin, born 9 August 1966, residing at Jovana Cvijica 29, Bosanski Samac, Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the entity known as Republika Srbska, is currently charged with a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions, pursuant to Article 2(c) of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (the Statute), a violation of the laws and customs of war, pursuant to Article 3(1)(a) of the Statute, and a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 5(i) of the Statute. On 14 February 1998, Milan Simic voluntarily surrendered himself to the Bosanski Samac police who then escorted him to the nearest International Stabilisation Force (SFOR) base where he was detained before being arrested by the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY). Since 15 February 1998, Milan Simic has been detained pending trial at the United Nations detention centre in The Hague, Netherlands. Through his Defence counsel, Drago Vukovic, Milan Simic has asked the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) to consider agreeing to his provisional release pending trial pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence (the Rules). Milan Simic contends that he qualifies for the exceptional circumstances provision of Rule 65(B) of the Rules due to his serious physical disabilities which have resulted in his confinement to a wheelchair. Pursuant to Rule 65(B) of the Rules, an accused may only be provisionally released 'in exceptional circumstances, after hearing the host country and only if [the Trial Chamber] is satisfied that the accused will appear for trial and, if released, will not pose a danger to any victim, witness or other person.' Furthermore, pursuant to Rule 65(C) of the Rules 'the Trial Chamber may impose such conditions upon the release of the accused as it may determine appropriate.' In response to a request for a provisional release pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules made by accused Milan Simic, the undersigned, as representatives of the entity known as Republika Srbska guarantee that should Milan Simic fail to comply with any of the conditions of his provisional release detailed on the attached document, the Ministry of Interior and all other relevant authorities of the Republika Srbska will execute and comply with any order pursuant to this request for provisional release issued by the Trial Chamber of ICTY and thereby ensure the return of Milan Simic to the seat of the Tribunal in The Hague for trial. Furthermore, the undersigned authorities of Republika Srbska agree to execute a bail bond in the amount of $US25,000 payable to the Registrar of the ICTY, as further assurance that the accused will return to The Hague as required by the Tribunal in relation to the charges detailed above. Said bail bond would become due on the date authorities of Republika Srbska fail to comply with this agreement. Should the undersigned or any other relevant authorities of the Republika Srbska fail to abide by this agreement, such failure will be reported immediately to the office of the High Representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Office of the High Representative then may undertake whatever actions it deems appropriate in regard to the failure of the representatives of Republika Srbska to abide by this agreement and SFOR will then have full authority to detain Milan Simic by whatever means necessary and thereafter transfer him as soon as practicable to the custody of the OTP of the ICTY for his return to The Hague." This document was signed by Milan Stankovic and Milorad Dodik. Unfortunately I am not sure of the exact date on which this document was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do we know the exact date? Mr Vukovic, do you know the exact date when this document was signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The document was signed on 20 March of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will add on to this document, "done on 20 March 1998 by a statement of Mr Vukovic, Defence counsel for Mr Simic." Any additional remarks that need to be made? The Chamber will rise. The ruling will be given during this morning and the Registrar will deal with that. (10.05)
